q: Which is an example of semi-structured data?
why: Page 6: semi-structured data has a flexible schema: JSON, XML, log files, common in APIs and NoSQL stores.

q: Which is structured data?
choices: A SQL table or time series of sensor values
why: Page 5: structured data fits rows and columns: tabular data, relational databases, time series.

q: Roughly what share of a data scientist's time goes into data preparation, per the deck?
why: Page 4: 60–70% of a data scientist's time goes into preparation, not modelling. 'Garbage in, garbage out.'

q: The deck's data-preparation pipeline, in order:
choices: Collect → inspect → clean → transform → store → visualize
Clean → collect → visualize → transform → inspect → store
Collect → transform → clean → inspect → visualize → store
Inspect → collect → store → clean → visualize → transform
why: Page 7: collect, inspect, clean, transform, store, visualize, as a repeatable pipeline.

q: Which pandas call gives summary statistics (mean, std, quartiles) during inspection?
why: Page 8: shape = row/column counts, dtypes = types, head() = quick look, describe() = summary statistics.

q: 'Tashkent', 'tashkent' and 'TASHKENT' in one column is which raw-data problem?
why: Page 9: inconsistency means the same value with different spellings.

q: A foreign key pointing to a record that no longer exists is called:
why: Page 9 lists six problems: missing values, duplicates, wrong format, outliers, inconsistency, broken relationships.

q: A column should have 1,000 values but only 950 are present. Completeness?
why: Page 16: completeness = available / expected × 100% = 950/1000 = 95%.

q: Which data-quality dimension asks 'Do values fall within an allowed range or format?'
why: Page 16's six dimensions: completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness, validity.

q: How are exact duplicate rows removed in pandas, and what catches near-duplicates?
choices: drop_duplicates(); record-linkage tools like recordlinkage or dedupe
why: Page 12: drop_duplicates() catches exact copies; near-duplicates (typos, formatting) need similarity-based record linkage.

q: A sensor briefly goes offline, so some readings are missing. Which mechanism?
why: Page 10: Missing Completely At Random means missingness has no relationship to any variable. The deck's example is a sensor going offline.

q: Older respondents skip the income question more often. Which mechanism?
why: Page 10: Missing At Random: missingness relates to other observed variables (here age).

q: High earners tend to hide their income. Which mechanism?
why: Page 10: Missing Not At Random: missingness depends on the missing value itself.

q: Which missingness mechanism does the deck call the hardest case?
why: Page 10: MNAR, because the reason a value is missing is the value itself, which you cannot observe.

q: Missingness depends on another column you can see (e.g. age). Students often call this MCAR. What is it?
choices: MAR: it depends on observed variables
MCAR: it is random within each age group
MNAR: it depends on the missing value
Not a missingness mechanism at all
why: The names mislead: 'At Random' (MAR) still means related to observed columns. Only MCAR is unrelated to everything.

q: Which imputation suits a categorical column like 'embarked'?
why: Page 11: mean/median for numeric columns, mode for categorical. The Titanic notebook fills 'embarked' with the mode.

q: What does IterativeImputer (MICE) do?
choices: Predicts each missing value from the other columns
Copies the value from the nearest row
Replaces missing values with the column mean
Drops every row that has a missing value
why: Page 11: IterativeImputer predicts each value from other columns (MICE). KNNImputer learns from nearest neighbours.

q: What does KNNImputer do?
choices: Fills a gap using the values of the most similar rows
Trains a GAN to generate missing values
why: Page 11: KNNImputer learns from the nearest neighbours. The Titanic notebook uses it for age (~20% missing).

q: In the Titanic notebook, 'deck' is 77% missing. What is done with it?
choices: Dropped, because too much is missing
why: Stage 1: deck (77% missing) is dropped; age → KNN imputer; embarked → mode; fare → median.

q: 'Drop every row that has a missing value' is listed by the deck as:
choices: A common mistake: diagnose the mechanism and choose a targeted strategy
The recommended default for all datasets
The only method that avoids data leakage
why: Page 36: dropping every row with a missing value throws away valuable data; diagnose MCAR/MAR/MNAR first.

q: Which is the deck's 'modern' deep-learning imputation approach?
why: Page 11: deep imputers such as GAIN and datawig learn non-linear patterns across many columns.

q: The IQR outlier fences are:
why: Page 13: IQR = Q3 − Q1; points below Q1 − 1.5·IQR or above Q3 + 1.5·IQR are outliers.

q: Q1 = 10, Q3 = 30. What are the IQR fences?
Q1 = 20, Q3 = 40. Is the value 75 an outlier by the IQR rule?
choices: Yes: anything above Q3 is an outlier
why: IQR = 20, 1.5 × 20 = 30, upper fence = 40 + 30 = 70. 75 > 70, so it is flagged.

q: Q1 = 4, Q3 = 8. Which value is flagged as an outlier?
why: IQR = 4, 1.5 × 4 = 6. Fences: 4 − 6 = −2 and 8 + 6 = 14. Only 15 is outside [−2, 14].

q: The Z-score is computed as:
why: Page 14: z = (x − μ)/σ, the number of standard deviations from the mean.

q: μ = 70, σ = 5. What is the z-score of x = 90, and is it an outlier?
why: z = (90 − 70)/5 = 4. The common cutoff is |z| > 3.

q: μ = 70, σ = 5. Z-score of x = 60?
why: z = (60 − 70)/5 = −2. Below the mean gives a negative z; |−2| < 3, so not an outlier.

q: What does the Z-score method assume, and what is its weakness?
choices: Roughly normal data; extreme outliers pull the mean and σ
No distribution at all; it is the most robust method
Uniform data; it cannot handle negative values
Categorical data; it needs one-hot encoding
why: Page 14: assumes approximately normal data and is sensitive to extreme outliers pulling the mean; combine with IQR when in doubt.

q: Which outlier method does NOT assume a normal distribution?
why: Page 13 calls IQR a robust, distribution-free rule of thumb. The Z-score assumes roughly normal data. (Page 13's 'roughly symmetric' wording is loose.)

q: How does Isolation Forest detect anomalies?
choices: Anomalies need far fewer random splits to isolate
It compares local density to neighbours' density
It flags points with high reconstruction error
why: Page 15: Isolation Forest splits randomly; anomalies get isolated in few splits. LOF is density-based; autoencoders use reconstruction error.

q: In the Titanic notebook, why are fare outliers clipped instead of deleted?
choices: First-class passengers genuinely paid high fares
The IQR rule cannot delete rows
why: Stage 4: clipping, not deletion, because the high fares are real. The checklist on page 37 also says: decide to fix, cap or keep.

q: Min-max normalization formula and output range:
why: Page 18: x' = (x − min)/(max − min), output in [0, 1].

q: min = 10, max = 50. Min-max scaled value of x = 30?
min = 0, max = 200. Min-max scaled value of x = 50?
μ = 60, σ = 10. Standardized value of x = 80?
Robust scaling: median = 40, Q1 = 30, Q3 = 50. Scaled value of x = 50?
After standardization, a feature has:
why: Page 19: output mean = 0, sd = 1. It does not bound the output, unlike min-max.

q: Rank the three scalers from most to least sensitive to outliers.
why: Page 20: min-max is very sensitive, Z-score sensitive, robust (median/IQR) resistant.

q: A feature has heavy outliers you don't want to delete. Which scaler?
why: Page 20 rule of thumb: start with standardization; switch to robust scaling when a boxplot/IQR check reveals heavy outliers. Titanic uses it for fare.

q: Which algorithms does the deck say min-max scaling is best for?
why: Page 18: best for neural networks, KNN and SVM, which are sensitive to the absolute scale of features.

q: Which models does the deck pair with standardization?
why: Page 19: best for linear and logistic regression, PCA and models assuming normally distributed inputs.

q: Does standardization remove outliers?
choices: No: an extreme value still distorts the mean and σ
Only if you use the median
why: Page 19 'watch out for': standardization does not remove outliers.

q: In the Titanic notebook, scaling barely changed random-forest accuracy (±0.5%). Why?
choices: Tree-based models are not affected by feature scale
The scaler was fitted on the test set
Random forests standardize inside each tree
why: The notebook's conclusion: normalization doesn't have much effect on RF because it is tree-based.

q: When is label encoding appropriate?
choices: Ordinal categories with a real order, e.g. small < medium < large
High-cardinality categories with hundreds of values
why: Page 21: label encoding is best for ordinal categories. On unordered ones it invents a false numeric relationship.

q: Tashkent = 0, Samarkand = 1, Bukhara = 2 fed into a linear model. What's wrong?
choices: It invents a false order: Bukhara looks 'twice' Samarkand
Nothing: label encoding suits city names
It leaks the target into the features
why: Cities are nominal. Page 36 lists label-encoding unordered categories as a common mistake; use one-hot instead.

q: One-hot encoding a 'city' column with 3 values (Tashkent, Samarkand, Bukhara) produces how many columns?
why: Page 21: one binary column per city (Tsh, Smk, Bkh). (pd.get_dummies with drop_first=True, as in the Titanic notebook, would keep 2.)

q: When is one-hot encoding the right choice?
choices: Nominal categories with a manageable number of values
Ordinal categories with a strict order
The target column of a regression
why: Page 21: one-hot for unordered categories with a manageable number of unique values.

q: What does target encoding replace each category with?
choices: The mean of the target for that category
why: Page 22: each category becomes the target mean, e.g. a city's average salary. Useful for high-cardinality columns.

q: Page 22 runs te.fit_transform(df, df['salary']) on the whole dataset. What's the problem?
choices: It leaks the target: fit the encoder on the training split only
Target encoding only works on numeric columns
Nothing; encoders are always fitted on all data
why: Fitting on the full data puts test-set target information into the features, breaking the deck's own golden rule on page 34.

q: For a very high-cardinality category inside a neural network, the deck's modern approach is:
why: Page 22: entity embeddings learn a dense vector per category and capture similarity between categories.

q: In the Titanic notebook, 'sex' is label-encoded but 'embarked' is one-hot encoded. Why is that fine?
choices: Sex is binary, so 0/1 adds no false order; embarked has 3 unordered values
Sex is ordinal; embarked is high-cardinality
Label encoding is always better for text columns
One-hot is needed only for columns with missing values
why: With two categories a single 0/1 column carries no fake ordering. 'embarked' has three nominal values, so one-hot.

q: 9,980 normal and 20 fraud transactions. A model always predicts 'Normal'. Accuracy?
why: 9,980/10,000 = 99.8%, yet it catches zero fraud. Accuracy lies on imbalanced data.

q: Which metrics does the deck recommend for imbalanced problems?
why: Page 24: evaluate with precision, recall, F1 or PR-AUC; standard accuracy rewards ignoring the minority class.

q: How does SMOTE create a synthetic sample?
choices: Pick a minority point, find its k nearest minority neighbours, interpolate between them
Duplicate a random minority point exactly
Delete random majority points until classes match
Flip, rotate or crop a minority example
why: Page 25: the four SMOTE steps; the new point is added to the training set.

q: Where should SMOTE be applied?
choices: On the full dataset before splitting
On both train and test so they match
why: Page 25: SMOTE only on TRAINING data; never resample the test set. Page 36 lists SMOTE on the test set as a common mistake.

q: Which SMOTE variant focuses new samples near the decision boundary?
why: Page 25: Borderline-SMOTE focuses near the boundary; ADASYN generates more for harder-to-learn minority examples.

q: Which alternative to resampling does the deck mention?
why: Page 25: class weighting / focal loss reweights the loss function instead of resampling.

q: Which feature-selection family scores each feature on its own, independent of any model?
why: Page 29: filter methods are model-independent: correlation, chi-square, ANOVA F-test, mutual information.

q: Recursive Feature Elimination belongs to which family?
why: Page 29: wrappers retrain the model repeatedly to test feature subsets: RFE, forward/backward selection, exhaustive search, BORUTA.

q: LASSO and random-forest importance belong to which family?
choices: Embedded methods: selection happens inside training
why: Page 29: embedded methods select features as part of model training.

q: Page 29 lists Ridge (L2) as an embedded selection method. Why is that loose?
choices: L2 shrinks weights but never makes them exactly zero; LASSO (L1) does
Ridge is a filter method, not embedded
Ridge only works on categorical features
Ridge removes the most important features first
why: Only L1 drives coefficients to exactly zero, which is what removes a feature.

q: Which is a feature-engineering transform the deck uses for a heavily skewed salary column?
why: Page 28: mathematical transforms; log(income) tames a skewed salary distribution.

q: In the Titanic notebook, family_size is built as:
why: Stage 5: siblings/spouses + parents/children + 1 (the passenger themself).

q: What is the deck's golden rule for scalers, encoders and imputers?
choices: Fit on train only, then transform both train and test
Fit on the full dataset, then split
Fit separately on train and on test
why: Page 34: any scaler, encoder, imputer or SMOTE call must fit() only on the training set; test gets transform() only.

q: You fit a StandardScaler on the whole dataset before the train/test split. Consequence?
choices: Test information leaks into training; metrics look better than in production
Nothing; the mean and σ are the same anyway
The model can no longer be trained
Only the test set gets scaled
why: Page 34: fitting on test data leaks information backward; evaluation looks great but the model fails in production.

q: How should a time series be split into train and test?
why: Page 34: never shuffle; split chronologically so the model is only tested on data after its training window.

q: What does a stratified split preserve?
choices: The class ratios in train and test
The time order of the rows
why: Page 34: stratified split preserves class ratios in imbalanced data (train_test_split(..., stratify=y)).

q: Which gives a more robust performance estimate than a single train/test split?
why: Page 34: k-fold cross-validation gives a more robust performance estimate.

q: What does Andrew Ng's 'data-centric AI' advocate?
choices: Improving the data (labels, coverage, noise) instead of only tuning the model
Always using the largest model available
Collecting data only from synthetic sources
Never cleaning the data, letting the model learn the noise
why: Page 30: systematically improve the data itself: fix mislabeled examples, add edge cases, remove noisy records.
